settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: For the varargs overload (line 69), the unsecured fast path requires verifiers.length == 0, so when any verifier is supplied that early-return path is not taken.
For the map overload (line 119), the unsecured fast path requires verifiers.isEmpty().
When a verifier is supplied and the token has 3 parts, line 149 throws MissingVerifierException rather than returning an unverified JWT.
VerifierTest only exercises correctly signed tokens, so no test demonstrates acceptance of an unsigned token with a signed alg.
candidates.description: JWTDecoder.decode(String, Verifier...) reads the algorithm solely from the untrusted header (line 66) and only treats a missing verifier as an error when the token has three parts: `if (parts.length == 3 && verifier == null) throw new MissingVerifierException(...)` (line 149). When the header declares a signed algorithm (e.g. HS256/RS256) and no supplied verifier can verify it, `verifier` stays null (lines 74-79 / 126-129); if the token has only two parts the guard at line 149 is not entered, the signature verification block at lines 153-157 is skipped, and the payload is deserialized at line 159 without any signature check. getParts accepts a two-part token only when the raw string ends with '.', i.e. the form `header.payload.` (an empty signature segment). The unsecured fast path that returns early (lines 69-71 and 119-121) is keyed off verifiers.length == 0 / verifiers.isEmpty(), not off header.algorithm, so it does not cover the case of a supplied-but-unmatched verifier. Root cause: the 'signature required' decision keys off parts.length == 3 instead of off whether the header algorithm denotes an unsecured token, and the 'accept unsecured' decision keys off the count of supplied verifiers instead of the header algorithm. Preconditions: the application calls decode() with a verifier map/varargs such that the looked-up verifier is null (unknown kid, or a verifier whose canVerify rejects the header algorithm), and the attacker supplies a token of the form header.payload. .
missing_evidence: No caller in this repository demonstrates a decoder invocation that could yield a null verifier for a two-part token.
Runtime behaviour of getParts on 'header.payload.' and of the subsequent JSON deserialization of the payload was not executed.
It was not verified that a three-part token with a null verifier cannot reach the payload deserialization by another route.
preconditions: Attacker can supply the encoded JWT string to a decode(...) call.
The verifier looked up by kid (map overload) is null, or the supplied verifier cannot verify the header-declared algorithm.
The crafted token has exactly two dot-separated segments and the raw string ends with '.' while its header claims a signed algorithm.
candidates.title: Two-part JWT whose header declares a signed algorithm may bypass signature verification and the missing-verifier error

counter_evidence: String.split on '.' for a canonical three-segment token yields the same boundaries as substring(0, lastIndexOf('.')), so for well-formed tokens message and signature segments agree.
Tokens with more than three split segments are rejected by getParts (length != 3 and not the 2-part-with-trailing-dot case).
The unsecured two-part path returns before reaching lastIndexOf/parts[2].
candidates.description: getParts (lines 174-182) accepts a token only as 'splits into exactly 3 parts' or '2 parts while the raw string ends with .'. The private decode method (lines 143-157) independently recomputes the signed message as `encodedJWT.substring(0, encodedJWT.lastIndexOf('.'))` (lines 143-146) rather than re-joining parts[0] and parts[1], and then uses parts[2] (line 153-155) as the signature segment. There is no guard cross-checking that the substring used as the signed message corresponds to the segments that were parsed. For canonical three-segment tokens the two computations coincide, and tokens with more than three split segments are rejected by getParts, so no divergence was demonstrated from source alone; the concern is that the signature is attributed to a byte range derived from a separate, differently-computed boundary than the segment the signature was taken from, which weakens the invariant between parsed structure and verified content. Reported as a robustness/consistency observation rather than a demonstrated bypass.
missing_evidence: No crafted input demonstrating an actual divergence between the substring used as the signed message and the parts[]-derived signature segment was executed.
No evidence that callers can pass a token with the required number of dots without an earlier validation layer rejecting it.
preconditions: Attacker controls the encoded JWT string passed to a decode(...) overload.
The token reaches the parts.length == 3 branch of the private decode method.
candidates.title: Signed message is recomputed with lastIndexOf('.') while the signature is taken from parts[2], so the verified byte range is not cross-checked against the parsed segments

counter_evidence: JWTUtils generates 32/48/64-byte HMAC secrets via SecureRandom and Base64, encouraging strong secrets.
No code path in the repository derives the HMAC secret from untrusted input; the value comes from configuration.
The library cannot evaluate the entropy of a caller-supplied secret.
candidates.description: HMACVerifier stores the supplied secret and uses it directly as the HMAC key with no minimum length, entropy, or algorithm-consistency check, while RSAVerifier/RSAVerifier-style construction enforces a minimum modulus length (2048-bit). The asymmetry means an application that derives an HMAC secret from a short password or low-entropy source could sign/verify tokens with a guessable key. This is a caller-configured risk, not a defect reachable from untrusted token input in this library: there is no code path here that derives the HMAC secret from token data, and JWTUtils provides SecureRandom-based secret generation. Reported as a design/robustness observation.
missing_evidence: No caller in this repository passes a caller-controlled short secret; the risk is contingent on downstream usage.
No specification in the repository states minimum HMAC key length requirements.
preconditions: Secret passed to HMACSigner/HMACVerifier is short or low-entropy.
Attacker can obtain at least one validly signed token to mount an offline guess.
candidates.title: HMAC key strength is not validated, unlike RSA modulus length which is enforced

counter_evidence: For signature-verified tokens, omitting exp is a decision of the issuer, not something an attacker can change.
The README usage examples always set an expiration, indicating intended usage includes exp.
The exp check does run whenever exp is present.
candidates.description: The decoder enforces only the exp and nbf checks after successful verification, and those are read from the token payload; absence of exp means the token is never considered expired and absence of nbf means it is always processable. There is no requirement that exp be present and no maximum-lifetime or iat/exp sanity check, so temporal policy is fully delegated to issuers/callers. For tokens that actually pass signature verification this is a policy choice rather than an attacker capability, so it is recorded as a design limitation.
missing_evidence: No documented security requirement in the repository mandates exp/nbf, and no configuration surface enforcing a maximum lifetime was found.
Reachability of the no-exp case through an external caller was not verified.
preconditions: The decoded token omits the optional exp and/or nbf claim, or carries a far-future exp.
The caller relies solely on decode() for token lifetime validation.
candidates.title: Token lifetime policy relies entirely on optional attacker-observable exp/nbf claims; no maximum lifetime or claim-presence requirement
